justice: The corridor is dominated by a narrow asphalt carriageway, while no dedicated sidewalk is visible for pedestrians, indicating uneven allocation of street space among users.
Several parked cars and trucks occupy the road edge, reducing usable space for other road users and weakening fair access to the corridor.
No curb ramps, tactile paving, marked crossings, or barrier-free pedestrian facilities are visible along the roadside, limiting accessibility for the general public.
The elevated expressway and fenced edge create a vehicle-oriented environment with little clearly provided public space for non-motorized users.
safety: There is no visible sidewalk or protected pedestrian zone, so anyone walking would need to share space with moving vehicles on the narrow road.
On-street parking by cars and trucks narrows the effective travel lane and may create sightline conflicts for approaching drivers and cyclists.
No lane markings, speed-control devices, crosswalks, or warning signs are visible, suggesting weak traffic organization and conflict management.
The underside of the elevated structure creates a darker edge condition that may reduce visibility and perceived security compared with an open, active street frontage.
livability: The street lacks visible shops, services, seating, or active ground-floor uses; instead, the edges are defined by dry vegetation, fencing, and infrastructure.
Large elevated-road infrastructure dominates the setting, giving the corridor a utilitarian rather than socially vibrant character.
No public gathering amenities such as benches, plazas, bus stops, or pocket green spaces are visible in the scene.
The roadside appears marginal and transitional, with vacant vegetated land on one side and fenced underpass space on the other, offering limited support for daily social life.
sustainability: No dedicated bicycle lane, bus stop, or other visible transit-supportive element is present, so the corridor appears to prioritize private motor travel.
Although roadside vegetation exists, it is mostly unmanaged dry grass and reeds rather than a clearly designed green infrastructure system.
The elevated structure provides some shade but also represents heavy car-oriented infrastructure with limited evidence of multimodal or low-carbon street design.
No visible stormwater features, permeable paving, or street trees are present to improve environmental performance at the street level.
aesthetics: The elevated viaduct visually dominates the scene and creates a harsh infrastructural edge with limited architectural or landscape refinement.
Dry roadside weeds, exposed fencing, and parked vehicles reduce visual order and weaken the overall streetscape quality.
The long perspective view and open sky provide some visual openness, preventing the scene from feeling completely enclosed.
A few distant houses and the linear structure create some spatial legibility, but the corridor still appears plain and utilitarian rather than attractive.
comfort: There are no visible benches, shelters, or resting facilities, so physical comfort for people stopping or waiting is very limited.
The absence of a proper sidewalk or buffer means pedestrians would experience low physical comfort while moving along the road edge.
The elevated roadway provides shade on one side, but the exposed left side with little tree canopy offers poor thermal comfort in sunny weather.
The stark infrastructure, fenced edge, and narrow mixed-traffic roadway may create psychological discomfort for users who feel exposed to vehicles and isolated space.
walkability: No continuous sidewalk is visible on either side of the road, which severely limits safe and convenient pedestrian movement.
There are no marked crosswalks, curb extensions, ramps, or pedestrian priority features to support route continuity.
Parked vehicles and trucks along the edge constrain walking space and force any pedestrian activity closer to moving traffic.
The corridor lacks active frontage, shade trees, and pedestrian amenities, making it unattractive for everyday walking.
bikeability: There is no designated bike lane, painted shoulder, or physical protection for cyclists on this roadway.
The narrow carriageway shared with cars and parked trucks would likely expose cyclists to overtaking and dooring risks.
No bicycle parking, bicycle signage, or intersection treatments for cycling are visible in the scene.
The straight alignment may aid visibility ahead, but the overall road design remains strongly motor-vehicle-oriented and offers little cycling support.
